title: 354 King Street North tower and Carnegie Library plans
subtitle: Siskins licence renewal, Carnegie museum design funding, Bill 5 concerns, and community event recognition.
overview: Council approved Official Plan Amendment 59 and Zoning By-law Amendment Z-24-15 for 354 King Street North {{vote:m6}}. The change allows a 24-storey apartment building with commercial space at street level. Its effective date depends on the provincial decision on a related amendment, OPA 58. Noise, wind, lighting and pick-up and drop-off concerns were referred to the later site plan stage.

Council also moved ahead with converting the vacant Carnegie Library into a museum. It approved a request for proposals for detailed design and released $930,000 in 2025 funding {{vote:m5}}. Staff will also pursue grants over the next two years. The building has sat empty for over a decade, so the work matters for a heritage site.

Council renewed the Kitchener-Waterloo Siskins licence for 2025-2026 {{vote:m4}}. Council spent the early part of the meeting in a closed session on accessibility orientation. Under new business, councillors raised concerns about Bill 5, a Lexington Road public meeting, and recognized community events, including the Service Centre open house, which raised money for Food4Kids.

decisions.detail: Council approved Official Plan Amendment 59 and Zoning By-law Amendment Z-24-15 for the site, with OPA 59 taking effect the day after the provincial decision on OPA 58.
Council directed staff to issue an RFP for detailed design of the museum renovation and released $930,000 in 2025 funding from the Capital Reserve Fund.
Staff will pursue relevant grants over the next two years, with any grant brought back to Council for approval.
Council directed staff to formalize a 2025-2026 licence renewal with the Kitchener-Waterloo Siskins Jr. B Hockey Club and authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign it.

debate: On the Carnegie Library, one councillor asked about heritage conservation and whether the building could hold a museum collection. Staff said the work involves repointing brick, checking the stone foundation, and upgrading windows and HVAC. The roof was recently replaced, and staff said similar reuses exist elsewhere.

A councillor urged qualifications-based selection instead of a standard RFP for the Carnegie design work, saying it had saved a large amount on the library project. Staff said they would score heritage expertise in the RFP. The Mayor treated the exchange as direction to look at the earlier procurement approach.

On the King Street North tower, councillors raised the reduced landscaped open space, delivery and ride-share vehicles stopping on King Street, and driveway turning movements near a bike lane. Staff said the Region accepted the driveways and will review them again at site plan, and that pick-up and drop-off would be addressed there.

Councillors also raised noise from the neighbouring drive-thru, wind on the north-side walkway and the rooftop terrace, and safety and lighting along the walkway. Staff said a holding symbol requires a detailed noise study first. The applicant's team said the wind study flagged only the upper part of the terrace. These items go to site plan.

Under new business, one councillor worried that Bill 5 would move pedestrian wind studies from the planning stage to site plan and remove some environmental permit requirements. The Mayor noted that staff had already sent comments to the environmental registry.
